newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: JOBS-S.Korea seeks labour deal, deadline nears.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-S.Korea seeks labour deal, deadline nears.

text.p: South Korea's politicians, business and labour are struggling to find common ground following labour unrest which unleashed a humiliating backlash for its leadership and undermined a slowing economy.
Labour chaos erupted in December after the ruling New Korea Party rushed labour reforms through parliament. The bill was passed in a clandestine dawn session while opposition deputies slept.
Under the new law, companies would be able to lay off surplus workers, hire temporary staff, and replace strikers.

The government argued that rigid work practices which virtually guaranteed jobs for life had raised costs and hampered South Korea's international competitiveness. Unions accused the government of wanting to turn workers into slaves.
Strikes forced the ruling party to send the bill back for further consideration and handed President Kim Young-sam a humiliating defeat in his last year in office.
"I feel sorry for worrying the public while revising the labour law last year," a chastened and solemn President Kim said in a televised address to the nation.
Although the legislation officially went into effect on March 1, the ruling and opposition parties have agreed to a deadline of March 8 for further review.
The work stoppages cost the nation $3.28 billion in lost production and $509 million in lost exports.
Some compromise has been achieved, however.

Union workers at struggling Ssangyong Motor Co, a unit of South Korea's Ssangyong Group, declared in January they would accept a wage freeze and give up all negotiations on working conditions until the company returned to the black.

Last month, Halla Group executives agreed to a 10 percent cut in pay in hopes of setting an example to other employees. The Samsung Group, which is not unionised, said it would freeze wages of executives and limit increases to below three percent for other workers.
Such measures were needed to boost performance in the midst of an economic slowdown while avoiding massive layoffs, company officials said.

"We must all share the pain," said Cho Jang-won, a Samsung Group spokesman. "This is one way to have job security, so that workers don't have to worry about when they or their friends will be fired." SOME PLAYERS YET TO BE WON OVER
But despite such moves toward compromise between individual companies and unions, other players seem set to remain spoilers.
The militant Korea Confederation of Trade Unions, which led the recent work stoppages, has called for more walkouts if the the national assembly's revisions to the law are not to their liking.
The Korea Employers Federation, which represents large conglomerates, said meantime its position on this year's wage negotiations will take into account production loss from recent strikes.
"If wage increases are too big, companies will be forced to lay off workers," federation spokesman Choi Jae-hwang said.
In South Korea, salary packages are traditionally negotiated in the spring.
Economists said labour reform was needed to meet the challenges of global competition.

"The lay-offs and the flexible working hours are the two essences of the labour law's effort to help the competitiveness of Korean companies," said Tae Chung, an economist at Jardine Fleming Securities in Seoul.

In 1996, the economy grew an estimated 6.9 percent, and economists predict it will expand 6.0-6.5 percent this year. This would be the weakest growth since 1980, when gross domestic product shrank 2.7 percent.
"If the nation's GDP falls bellow 6.5 percent, we may see an increase in the unemployment rate," said Cho Yoon-je, senior counsellor to the minister of finance and economy.
The unemployment rate rose to 2.4 percent in January, from 1.9 percent the previous year, government figures show.
While the economy's slowdown is blamed mainly on falling semi-conductor prices, rapid increases in wages have also dulled the nation's competitive edge. PAY RISES OUTPACE PRODUCTIVITY GAINS
From 1985 to 1995, salaries rose by a real 14.2 percent, while productivity gains lagged behind at 11.2 percent, the Korea Labour Institute said.
Even as ruling and opposition parties seek a compromise on labour reform, their efforts have been accompanied by significant distractions.
A loans-for-kickbacks scandal sparked a major cabinet reshuffle this week, producing a new prime minister and finance minister as seven ministerial portfolios changed hands.
